utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you. Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it that you are following what I am saying in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take your place. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland, together with Denise Gustin, case manager for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm David Cunningham. Today I'm assisted by Aleksandar Vujic, and we have some preliminaries, at the Court's convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we remain in open session for the time being. And yes, who is going to go first? Ms. Sutherland, do you have any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So then it's Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yesterday, Your Honour, the Court wanted a written response to the government's motion dealing with the scheduling. Mr. Ackerman has filed such a motion. I've given a courtesy copy to the registrar. Basically, our position is with respect to the reduction of one-week time in this final arguments, we have no objection to that. We are going to keep our case length the same length, and we would oppose any reduction in the time to file our final briefs from four weeks to three weeks. And that's all set out in the motion that was provided to the Court. The Court also asked me to determine for Mr. Ackerman what our position would be with respect to an extension with respect to the brief due at the end of the government's case. He is filing a motion and respectfully asking the Court for an additional one week to do that brief, and that's the second preliminary matter that I wanted to bring to the Court's attention. And a motion is being filed on that this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The third matter that I want to bring to the Court's attention deals with the witness that we're dealing with today. My recollection is this witness does not have any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my recollection, too. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It is referenced in this witness's statement that he gave to the OTP that he was working on a book that he sought to get published. Yesterday when they proofed him it is my understanding that he brought with him a 172-page-long B/C/S only transcript of his recounting the events surrounding this municipality. We certainly didn't have enough time to get that translated last night. Mr. Ackerman has taken that to the Translation Service today. What I would propose to do, and if the Court agrees, I'm going to do as much cross-examination as I can today. When we get the document, if there's anything needed, we would alert this Court to that fact, but I'm prepared to move forward, as far as I can with as much as I can in the absence of that book, journal, whatever he would like to call it. But I would like to have the opportunity to review that document and have the opportunity, if additional cross-examination is needed, to call him back. And we would be certainly willing to do that during our case. And the reason I bring that up with our case is I'm discovering that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Mr. Cunningham. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Because I understand that the backlog facing the Translation Services, sometimes it can take a while to get the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Sutherland, do you have anything to say or to state with regard to what Mr. Cunningham --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I agree with what Mr. Cunningham has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I can confirm here now, because if you don't agree, let me know, but the position is this: You certainly have a right and we recognise that right that if this document has been forwarded to you only between yesterday and today, and it needs to be translated before you can really understand it, then that will be taken into consideration. You will have a right either to cross-examine the witness during your case, if you're not in a position to cross-examine him during the Prosecution's case, or else you are also free to ask for his production, to be brought forward here and be one of your witnesses. You can also do that. And if that is the case, more or less the procedure here is very flexible. There isn't much difference between the Rules governing examination-in-chief and cross-examination. So more or less I can guarantee you every opportunity that you need to have this witness brought over again for any cross-examination or examination-in-chief, if necessary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we're clear, I don't think Mr. Cunningham wants the witness to become his witness during his case, but just cross-examination will occur during his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that was the point that I was trying to make. I don't have any intention to call him. I was just thinking if there's additional cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I'm telling you that you're also free to call him if you feel that he can be of assistance to you. It has been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I understand it's been done, but I don't think this is going to be of use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But you will have every opportunity to have him brought over again to have him cross-examined even during your case. So Ms. Sutherland, do you think we can proceed with the witness in open session without any problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He doesn't request any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's bring in the next witness. And in the meantime, Mr. Cunningham, I don't know if you have been served with this, but do you remember there was a Prosecution motion to exempt specific material from immediate disclosure, a request for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were given an inter parte --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We filed a motion ex parte, but we advised the Defence in an inter parte motion that we had filed an ex parte motion with you. But we filed the withdrawal of the motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's what I was going --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- inter parte simply to advise both the Chamber and the Defence at the same time that we were withdrawing the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Your Honour, there is a decision on protective measures outstanding for the witness who is going to be testifying next Monday. That is in relation to BT94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: BT94. Reinhold, will you look into that? And there is, Mr. Cunningham, before the witness -- the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is another motion which was filed on the 16th of June, asking for protective -- certain protective measures regarding Witness BT97. If you could perhaps in the course of today's sitting inform us. There is no mention of a closed session, so there shouldn't be --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There shouldn't be any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is that with respect to BT 94 and 97?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. This is with respect to BT 97 only what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll let the Court know at the end of the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. This was filed on the 16th of this month. Good morning, Mr. Cirkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear what I am saying being interpreted in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that makes things easier, because it's one of the most important things. You're here to give evidence. You know that. And you are about to start giving evidence in the trial against Radoslav Brdjanin. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, you enter a solemn declaration, practically an oath, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher, who is standing next to you, is going to give you the text of the solemn declaration. Please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. Make yourself comfortable. Make yourself comfortable and let's proceed. Have you ever given testimony before in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think I had better explain to you a little bit what's going to happen, which is pretty much a simple procedure. You see that there are two parties in this trial, the Prosecution and the Defence, and they both have a right to ask you questions, and that's what's going to happen today. Corresponding to this right, you have an obligation, once you have accepted to come forward and give evidence, to answer all the questions that are put to you as fully and as truthfully as possible, in line with the solemn undertaking that you have just made, and I'm sure you understand me. And this duty, this obligation, arises not only from the solemn declaration, but also because each party has the right to know the truth and to get the truth out of you. So you have no right to draw or to make any distinctions between questions coming from the Prosecution or questions coming from the Defence. Your duty is to answer all questions, irrespective of where they are coming from, as fully and as truthfully as possible. You will first be asked questions by Ms. Sutherland, who I suppose you have met already, and she will then be followed by Mr. Cunningham. If you have any problems in the course of your testimony, if you are feeling tired, you'd like to rest, just tell me and we will have a rest. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: My name is Rasim Cirkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, there's something wrong now with my -- I think it needs to be changed. It just went dead completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can the interpreters say something, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. One, two, three. One, two, three. One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I am not receiving anything. It suddenly went dead completely. I'm not receiving anything. We can proceed. I mean, I don't mean to -- no, no, no. It's everything is in order except that it's not coming through. It was coming through and then I heard a sound and that was it. I thought it was the headphones, but it's not the headphones. It's the set here. But in any case, I can follow on the monitor. Please proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Cirkic, you were born on the 28th of March, 1957?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's coming through now. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Dabovci Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's in the Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your ethnicity is Muslim?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're married, with two children, aged 22 and 20?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You attended primary school in Vrbanjci, in Kotor Varos municipality, and completed secondary school in Banja Luka in 1975?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You performed compulsory JNA military service in 1976 and 1977, and you were attached to the Atomic/Biological/Chemical branch of the army, located in Krusevac, Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you worked in the decontamination department?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 1977 you became a civil servant in the army, and you worked in the military barracks Precko in Zagreb in the military warehouse?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also worked in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With the military. Did you work in any other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You ended up as manager of the warehouse and you worked there until September 1991, when you left the army after the war in Croatia began?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were a member of the Communist Party until 1989, and after that you did not become a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're currently employed as a factory worker; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague, you had an opportunity to review your statement that you gave to members of the Office of the Prosecutor, and you made three minor changes to that statement?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now want to turn to events which occurred in the Kotor Varos municipality in 1992.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you returned from Croatia to the village of Cirkici in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there a radio or television station in Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: There was no television station in Kotor Varos. We were taking over the programme from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up or come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please raise your voice so the interpreters can hear what you're saying. Was there a radio station in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At that time, September 1991, what television transmissions did you receive? You mentioned a moment ago, I think, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please come closer to the microphones and speak up. We can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you just move your chair in a little bit closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive television transmissions from any other place but Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the nature of the programmes?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: These programmes were by and large about crimes committed against the civilian population in Croatia and how the Yugoslav People's Army was trying to defend Yugoslavia, so that it was a propaganda programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the programmes change at all?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: All these programmes were very similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did this intensify between September 1991 and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you give the Court some examples of what you saw on the television?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I can't do it right now. I just can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the non-Serb residents believing what they saw on the television?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, in your view, was the primary objective of what was being televised?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The spreading of untruths about the real events.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there TV programmes about things which were occurring in other municipalities within the Autonomous Region Krajina, for example, in Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I only followed one case in a place called Hambarine, which is near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was shown on the television about Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They showed a group of Bosniaks and Croats who wanted to take over power in Prijedor, in the municipality of Prijedor. These people were depicted as extremists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to a different topic. Do you know Radoslav Brdjanin personally?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever see Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was that you first saw Radoslav Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I think it was towards the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you see him on television?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, but I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the nature of the programme in which you saw Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I think they were the programmes of political parties or political party activists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: There was a campaign for Banja Luka to become the capital of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to another topic, and that is the arming of the Serb and Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the Muslim population purchasing weapons?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were purchasing weapons, but in small quantities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were they purchasing the weapons from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they purchased weapons from Serbs, that is to say from reservists who were returning from the front and who would sell those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of weapons they were purchasing?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Mainly small arms, semi-automatic and automatic rifles, and small quantities of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Serbian population were being armed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court how you -- what you saw?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The people going to join the reserve forces, they would return with automatic rifles and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And these weapons weren't being returned to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the weapons that were stored in the TO building?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were transferred to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that to the JNA barracks in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point did you start night patrols in your village or other Muslim villages that you know of?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why did you do this?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Serbian reservists starting entering Muslim and Croatian villages and spreading panic among the population. This happened during the day, and one incident I can remember is when a number of reservists went to the village of Bilice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting that was held on or about the 8th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the reason for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We wanted to avoid a war at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: There was a group of about a hundred people, Croats and Bosniaks. Three representatives of the JNA and a local man who was the representative of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the situation like during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It was very tense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the outcome of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive any of the guarantees that we had requested. We were even threatened. We were told that if something happened, we would be to blame for everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the guarantees that you were seeking?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We had asked for guarantees that there wouldn't be any attacks from the side. We asked for the army units to withdraw, the ones that were positioned around Maslovare. And we also asked for excessive behaviour and uncontrolled behaviour of reservists to stop, that took place in the village of Vrbanjci --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please repeat the names of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters have asked you to repeat the names of the villages. They didn't quite hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The local commune of Maslovare, if you're referring to the place where the units were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then I think you asked for excessive behaviour and uncontrolled behaviour of reservists to stop, and that was taking place in the village of Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the village of Vrbanjci, groups of reservists often appeared. They were drunk and they would behave in an uncontrolled manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And these are Serb reservists you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you conclude from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I personally expected something to happen at any moment. The situation was extremely tense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when power was taken over by the Serbs in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th of June, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I was in Cirkici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where is Cirkici located?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: North of Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P2120. It's the ethnic composition map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, using the pointer that's beside you on the -- looking at the map on the machine which is to your right, can you point on the machine to your right your village where you lived in Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If that map can stay there. We will be using that shortly. Can you describe for the Court what you saw from your village that morning?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Around dawn, Ramic Safet and his family appeared in my village. He had a large family. They came with a TAM lorry and they said that Vrbanjci had been occupied. After several minutes, another man appeared and he confirmed this. And at about 10.00, from Vrbanjci, a group of civilians from Vrbanjci headed towards Cirkici. They passed through Bara at the river of Bosanka, and headed towards my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, Cirkici, the topography, is that situated on a hill?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The village goes from the river to Cirkino Brdo. It's on a slight slope.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that river goes from Vrbanjci to which village?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It goes from Plitska towards Rujevica. It separates Hanifici between Cirkici and Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, from your village, approximately how much of the Kotor Varos municipality would you be able to see?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: From one place in Cirkino Brdo, you can see about 80 per cent of the municipality of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that early that morning, on the 11th of June, Vrbanjci had been attacked. What about the town of Kotor Varos? Were you able to see anything there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Not at the time, but after a while, from the direction of Kotor Varos, smoke appeared from a number of houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: By the end of the day, how many refugees from Vrbanjci had come to Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number, but between 300 and 400 people. That would be my assessment. They were mainly women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Had they been told by anybody to go to Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They all said that a Serbian officer had directed them to Cirkici. At least, that's what they told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Kotor Varos and Vrbanjci, they were both on the main road between Banja Luka and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what is that part of -- what was that part of the country referred to in 1992, that road between Banja Luka and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I think they called it the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, the men from Vrbanjci, where did they seek the shelter? Did they all stay in Cirkici or did they move somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They first went to Hanifici, and then in the evening they moved on to Cirkici, from Hanifici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to see from your village the actual attack or were you just told about it when the men came from Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't see combat vehicles entering Vrbanjci itself. I only heard this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened on the 12th of June?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The attack on Hrvacani began on the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to see this from your village?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: First of all, we heard the sound of shots, and then we saw that a building was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How far, approximately, as the crow flies, is it between Cirkici and Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is it the next village, the next big village to the east of Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see --

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It would be the north-east.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to see how this village was attacked?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We heard shooting from various firearms. At the beginning it was infantry, from infantry weapons. Then we could hear mortars, and probably anti-aircraft machine-guns, because you could hear bursts of fire and you could see bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is it that you recognised the noises that you were hearing because of your experience in the army?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Other schools recognise the use of recoilless cannons or anti-aircraft machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw a building on fire. Was there more than one building?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what you saw?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We first saw a building on fire, and you could see the flames and smoke coming out of it, and several minutes later -- we didn't see flames in the other houses, because part of the village of Hrvacani is on the opposite side -- is opposite to the slope, so you could only see the smoke coming out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see any infantry into the village?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could see how the infantry was approaching the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did they do when they entered the village?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: First, tractors started coming out, and some lorries with equipment on them. And then there was more and more smoke, more and more flames coming out of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did the Muslim population from that village do?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They moved to the neighbouring Croatian village, to Plitska. They passed through an area, first the civilians went, the women and children, and in the early evening the men followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Later that day, did you see any Serb soldiers entering the village of Hanifici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately what time did that occur?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, at about 4.00, but I don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the inhabitants still in the village?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't. Some of them had already gone to Cirkici, and others to Plitska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see what the soldiers did in the village of Hanifici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: First, one house, Botic Galib's house, was set on fire, and then several other houses. Between 17 and 20 houses were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, 1992, what did you see happening on that day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was Plitska attacked at all?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was attacked. Plitska was attacked one day after Hrvacani had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you -- looking at the map, P2120, we can see the -- where you pointed to the village of Cirkici, and we can see Hrvacani next to that, and Hanifici just below Cirkino Brdo.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then Plitska, which is to the north-west of Cirkino Brdo.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you've just told us that as these villages were being attacked - and we can also see Vrbanjci down on the river --

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- which is directly south from Cirkino Brdo. When all these refugees, when all these -- I'm sorry, when all these villages were being attacked and refugees were going from one village to the next, did a lot of refugees end up in Cirkino Brdo, Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the refugees from Hrvacani, Hanifici, and from Plitska finally ended up in Cirkino Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did anyone try and negotiate with the Serbs about the refugees?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Three persons tried to establish contact with the Serbs in Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the outcome of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The outcome of the meeting was that two of them returned, and a third person was detained by the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you told to surrender your weapons?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many, and what type of weapons were surrendered?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Several automatic rifles, several hunting rifles, and some ammunition. We didn't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you possess a weapon?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you surrender it?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't trust them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you come to know of a massacre which occurred in Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: A man appeared in my village, someone who lived in Vrbanjci. His name was Camko Hadziric. And he stayed with Hamdzic Zifon [phoen] and I found out about the massacre from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: He said that he and a group of seven or eight men had been taken to the centre of Vrbanjci, to a cafe, and they were ordered to go to Malovo [phoen] and to collect some bodies. Camko Hadziric recognised his son on that occasion and some other people, and he told me the names of other people who had been killed. The group with which Camko carried out this task never appeared again, the group with which he collected these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what happened to Camko?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: About ten days later, ten days after Camko had appeared in my village, a Serbian patrol appeared and took him away. They said that Balaban needed him and Camko never appeared again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was Balaban?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know who Balaban was. I found out who he was later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Nenad Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I met Balaban in Kotor Varos, in the police station. He introduced himself as the chief of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From your village, were you also able to see the attack on Vecici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also the attack on Sokoline?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you briefly tell the Court what you saw in relation to the attacks on those two villages.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: For several evenings in a row, fire was opened from mortars, and I believe recoilless guns, from the Serb village of Serdari, and it went on day after day after day, irrespective of the time of the day. And then one day they turned up from the direction of Uzlomac, between Cirkici and Hanifici. The planes came up and bombed Vecici. Six planes came, five opened fire on Vecici, and the sixth returned to Kotor Varos and fired rockets on the village of Sokoline. The planes were flying low so that one could easily see the markings on them, to know who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The markings were the markings of the Yugoslav People's Army, and there was a flag of the former Yugoslavia on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point did you go to the village of Vecici; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. A few days later, yes, I was in Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I couldn't see a single house standing up and intact. All the houses had been shelled and damaged. I saw craters made by bombs of major destructive power. The scars left by flames. And what attracted my attention was part of the forest where all the leaves had fallen off. And at that time of the year, I mean, you couldn't see a forest, a leafless forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The villages that we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sutherland, because this calls for a further question for sure. What is your explanation or your conclusion when -- or what was your conclusion or your explanation when you noticed that all the leaves had fallen off, the time of the year when they should be on the tree? Did you come to any conclusion? And if you did, what did you base it upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My conclusion was that a chemical must have been used, and this was then confirmed by people who lived there and said that after they had been bombed, had certain health problems. That is, they were all coughing. And they said that there was a lot of smoke after they had been bombed, and that's why I decided those must have been some gases, some poisons, some irritants which made people cough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The village, did you hear from others whether women were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard how the Serb units, when entering Vecici, got some 20 minutes and forced them to walk in front of them and made them walk in front of them as they entered Vecici [as interpreted]. Those women were not allowed to leave immediately. They were taken back to Vrbanjci and then transferred to Obodnik, and only from there were they taken back to Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The villages that we've mentioned, Vrbanjci, Vecici, Hanifici, Hrvacani, that were all attacked, they're all Muslim villages, aren't they, predominantly Muslim people lived in those villages in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Hrvacani was 100 per cent Muslim; Cirkino Brdo, likewise; Hanifici, likewise. In Hanifici there were some Serbs and Croats, but the majority was Muslim, and Plitska was a hundred per cent Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Sokoline is also majority Croat population, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As a result of these attacks on the villages, was any sort of defence set up in your village?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: At the outset, we had no military formations. We merely tried to defend -- to protect the population, so that we organised ourselves and decided that if we saw that some units were coming, that we should pull out the -- evacuate the population into the woods. So that we didn't have any army formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many were in this defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: There were not very many people who were fit for combat. Only about 18 people. The rest were either elderly or young people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this group of 18, how many weapons did they have between them?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Hardly any. We had some three hunting rifles. I believe there was one automatic, one semi-automatic rifle, and a few pistols, and very little ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your group or any other groups that had been set up to defend their villages capture any Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, not in the early days, but later on, a group captured four Serb soldiers in the area of Kotor. It's in the municipality of Kotor Varos, that is, a part of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did you take the Serb soldiers that were captured?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They were taken over and -- taken and handed over in Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the circumstances? How did you capture them? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Since they came from a part of Kotor Varos, from a part of Kotor, people who had fled to local Croat villages, and they were coming back every day to get some food or clothes or something, because people had taken first initially only basic necessities. So that group had gone back to get some food and some other necessities, and they captured four Serb soldiers who were, I think, in a vehicle which was either an ambulance car or what. I don't know exactly, because I didn't see that car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any of your -- were any Muslims or Croats killed during this attack -- this incident?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: A few days earlier, perhaps a day or two, a group of seven, eight Croats and Muslims was killed in the area of Kotor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. He's not picked up your question, Ms. Sutherland. Ms. Sutherland asked you whether on this occasion when you captured the four Serb soldiers, any of your own got killed. Not days before, but on that specific occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I give him back to you, because you have a problem now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know of a man called Sprdjo?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Sprdjo was one of the people in the group that I mentioned a moment ago, who was killed. His body wasn't found with the other bodies. It had been taken to Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was done with his body in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: In Kotor Varos, Sprdjo was put on a combat vehicle and drove him around in order to show how they had caught a major figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where was he driven to?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Banja Luka or Maslovare. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was this televised?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see that programme, but I heard from other people that it was shown on television. I heard it from Sprdjo's nephew, who buried him after his body was returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened to the four Serb soldiers that were captured?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I heard that Minja, the name of one was Minja, and the others, I don't know. I didn't have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you don't know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Redjo Vatrac?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Vatrac. Could I hear the last name again, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Redjo Vatrac.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I know him. He's my wife's brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was he killed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the circumstances in him being killed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Redjo and a group of four or five men were intercepted in a Croat village, and there was an exchange of fire. Redjo returned to a house which was set on fire by a bomb. I suppose that is what happened, because we found there a body which had been charred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now to the 14th of August, 1992. On that day, were the villages -- the people in the villages of Vrbanjci and Cirkici rounded up?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cirkici was surrounded during all this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I wasn't clear in my question, but I will go back. Between when the takeover occurred on the 11th of June, 1992, until the 14th of August, 1992, are you saying that the village of Cirkici was surrounded all of that time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: If you look at the map, you will see that there is a Serb village behind it. On the other side is Serdari, on the other side, Vrbanjci. So that we could not really move far away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did there come a time when all these civilians from villages surrounding Vrbanjci were all rounded up?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Some of the civilians from Vrbanjci came to Cirkici and stayed there for a while. Some of them returned to Vrbanjci and then came back to Cirkici once again. And part of the population had moved over to Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point did the Serbs start rounding up all the civilians, the women, the men, the children, the elderly?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and they brought them to the petrol pump, an unfinished one in Vrbanjci, near a place called Lipa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to the population at that point?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That population was taken in the direction of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the men separated from the women and the children?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see any men among those civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were the women and children taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They were taken in different vehicles in the direction of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you become aware of a large number of men who were killed at Cejvani and Lihovici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. I learnt that later, when I was captured, from a man who was brought to this later, whose name was Alija Cejvan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he told you about this?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right. He told me about this at some point. He told me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At one point you mentioned just a moment ago that you were captured. Can you just briefly describe the circumstances in which you were captured?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: When we saw them rounding up the civilians in neighbouring villages and taking them to the above-mentioned place, I and a few other guys tried to evacuate our civilians towards Bilice, which is a Catholic, a Croat locality, behind the forest, to prevent their being taken away too. And I personally tried to be as active as I could about getting those civilians together and sending them to Bilice. And at that moment, I was arrested. I approached a group of some 20 individuals, and some of them were elderly men, and young men, and women. I did not want to frighten them by appearing with a pistol that I normally carried, and a grenade which I had, so that I left them by a bush not far from the place where those people were sitting. And at that moment, I told them that they should not be there and that they should start moving slowly towards Bilice. And I was still talking, because those people told me that nobody would harm them there, that they were free there, and I was trying to tell them something else, trying to convince them. And then I heard some movement behind my back, and then I tried to get away. I tried to jump across a fence, across some wire. And as I did that, I literally ran, bumped into the barrel of an M-53, which is a machine-gun. And at that moment, I heard the order to surrender, and at that moment I didn't know what to do. So that -- Your Honours, I'd rather not talk about those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The microphone is on. The microphone is on. Maybe I need to come nearer, but the microphone is on. I fully understand. Ms. Sutherland, we can, I suppose, take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and then I will be moving straight to the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would suggest to you if Mr. Cunningham has got nothing against, the next few pages in his statement go into great detail how he was tortured, beaten, and beaten again and beaten again and tortured and beaten again and again and again. We could spare the gentleman all this, if you would agree that this part of the statement, only, will be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to lead this evidence out of the witness. It goes directly to implicate a member of the Crisis Staff, and it's important that this evidence is heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No, no. It's okay. But you are going to have problems, obviously. So anyway, I'll give you an opportunity to think about this. We'll reconvene in 25 minutes' time, and we see how we go about it. But, on the other hand, sir, you are going to have a break now and have a coffee and relax a little bit. I know it's not easy to relive these events that you are telling us about, but also we need to know. So let's have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin is here. Ms. Sutherland, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before you proceed, two things: I should like you to, to your utmost, both of you, to finish this witness today. The reason is that this witness was scheduled to last one day in any case, number one. Secondly, the Defence requires roughly about 30 minutes for cross-examination, so you regulate your in-chief accordingly. Then we have another witness laid out, I assume, for tomorrow. We don't need to mention names. He was also scheduled to testify for one day here, which leaves us a big question mark that I would like to know about as far as Friday is concerned. Do you have anyone else already prepared in line for Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were trying to bring a witness forward for Friday, but that looks like it's not possible now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's not, please ask Ms. Korner or liaise with Ms. Korner, and perhaps you can bring forward Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't know whether he's in the office at the moment, Your Honour, this week. But the other thing that might be of assistance is to read the diary of Witness 7.207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean read it here in open Court?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, no, no, Your Honour, but to use that time. Because the witness will be testifying on Monday, and it is a rather lengthy document, and I don't know whether Your Honours have had the opportunity to go through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not all of it. Not all of it. I speak for myself. I have started, but it can be done over the weekend as well. And the idea when we had the meeting in my office last week was possibly for that witness -- Ms. Korner herself suggested that she could well file, tender as an exhibit the diary and not ask any questions at all, and leave the witness in the hands of Mr. Ackerman for cross-examination. The point is this: What is important for me is not who comes on Friday. What is important for me is that we do not waste a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, you're free to regulate your own procedure accordingly, and according to your needs. But please don't let us -- don't put us in a position where we have to waste one day or one morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We've -- the witnesses this week have gone much quicker than we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's better, that's a good sign. The witness is in your hands, Ms. Sutherland. I leave it up to you how to go through the rest of the events in which he was so directly involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown a number of photographs. The first one, Exhibit P2320.8, which has the ERN number 0203-3384.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You can see a mosque that has been destroyed in the village of Vecici, and some houses. As far as I can remember, during the war, these houses didn't have any roofs, so this photograph doesn't come from that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. These photographs, I think, Your Honours, were taken last year -- in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the next photograph, which is Exhibit P2320.9, ERN 0203-3385.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You can see a mosque in this photograph. Its minaret has been destroyed. I think it's also in Vecici. In Vecici, Your Honours, there were two mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph, P2320. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sutherland. The word "two mosques". Were they both destroyed or was this one only that was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were both destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown the next exhibit, P2320.15, ERN number 0203-3397.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: This is from Cirkin Brdo, across the road from Bosanka. It's a view of the village of Hanifici. You can also see that some of the houses here had been restored or renovated, that these houses didn't have any roofs when I left that area. So this photograph must also be fairly recent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next Exhibit, P2320.14, with the ERN number 0203-3398.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: This is also a mosque in the village of Cirkici and Hanifici. This was a joint mosque, a common mosque. This photograph was taken from the rear, at the rear of the mosque. It wasn't the front of the mosque, facing the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And lastly, if the witness could be shown P2320.13, ERN number 0203-3395.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's the same mosque, but from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is the minaret visible in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You can see the minaret on the left side of the building. It's on the ground. It has been toppled over. Part of the minaret remained on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the photograph which is P2320.1, ERN number 0203-3371.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You can see the remains of the Catholic church, the Croatian church, in Kotor Varos. You can quite clearly see this part with the cross, which is on the left side of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2320.20, ERN number 0203-3445.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You can see the new police station in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We are going to talk about your detention very, very shortly. Can you point on that photograph --

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I was brought in from the direction of the street. I was taken up to this point, to the steps. And on this side of the steps, there were sand bunkers. I was stopped here. There was a group of a number of soldiers wearing uniforms which were slightly different from those of others. They had white belts with the letters "CSB," Security Services Centre. I was stopped here and I was ordered by one of them who had brought me there in a car to greet the men. I said good day. I thought that that was our traditional greeting. But I was told that that was not the way to greet them, that I was supposed to say "God help you, heroes." And they started beating me then, so I'm not sure whether I really greeted them in this way or not. I was then ordered to go a few steps back, but the people who were there lined up. They formed a sort of corridor that I had to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't know if he's done with his question, but my objection was going to be that it was totally non-responsive to pointing on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have asked the witness to describe what happened when he was taken to the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it can remain as it is, because the question was: "We are going to talk about your detention very, very shortly. Can you point on that photograph," and the question stopped there, and it was the witness who picked up the rest. So I think it is -- I feel it is all in order and we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would have come to that in any case. Yes, Ms. Korner -- Ms. Sutherland. You haven't become an obsession as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, after you were made to -- what happened as you went through this cordon of policemen? You said that they started beating you.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened when you got through the cordon of people? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They took me to a room. When you go up these steps, there's a small corridor and there's a sort of reception area there. I was detained there briefly. They then took me to another room, and then someone who introduced himself as Inspector Zdravko appeared. He said that he was to question me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, I've finished with that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The person who took you to the office, do you know the name -- his name?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He introduced himself as Dule Vujicic. I don't know whether that's his real name or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, when you entered this room and a man introduced himself as Inspector Zdravko, did he start to question you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: He asked me who I was, where I was from. He asked me about my family, whether I was married, et cetera. He asked me why I had been arrested and what kind of weapons I had. And then there were questions that I had never thought about before. He also asked me how many Serbian civilians I had killed, how many Serbian women I had raped, how many Serbian children I had killed, how many Serbian women I had raped. Your Honours, I would never have dreamed of such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was Inspector Zdravko --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Zdravko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- asking you these questions or was somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Zdravko asked me these questions, but while he was asking me these questions, there was a policeman or two policemen who were constantly present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did anyone else enter the room?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: After a while, two persons entered. One has already been mentioned, Vujicic. And the other person introduced himself as Slobodan Dubocanin. They were both in camouflage uniforms. Slobodan Dubocanin's uniform was slightly different. The colour was slightly different and its shape was slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What colour was his uniform?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It was a little greener. The other policeman was in a blue camouflage uniform, whereas this one had a greenish uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First I want to ask you about these three men. Did you know a person called Dule Vujicic before you saw him that day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know Inspector Zdravko?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe him for me?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: At the time he was about 35 years old, of medium height. He was quite well built, quite strong. He was in uniform. He had a shirt, and his sleeves had been rolled up. He had a camouflage uniform, but the sleeves had been rolled up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Slobodan Dubocanin, did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe him for me?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Dubocanin was taller than Zdravko and he was quite -- he had an athlete's build. He looked like a good sportsman, or at least that was the impression I had at the moment. At that time, I think he was about 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What colour hair?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I think it was fair. I think he was fair, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When he entered the room, what happened?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: He asked me very briefly where I was from, who I was, where I had been arrested, and then he started interrogating me, because apparently I hadn't provided Zdravko with the right information. So I was asked a series of questions again. Your Honours, I tried to answer those questions as best I could at the time, but whatever the answer I provided, they weren't satisfied and then they started beating me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They punched me, they kicked me. Someone said that I shouldn't be hit over the head. I don't know who. And then I had the impression that someone was a sportsman, because I was dealt fierce blows in the back, in the chest, and so on. I was in great pain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any of the three men armed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that two of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which two?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Dubocanin and Dule Vujicic. Zdravko was sitting on the other side, and I didn't notice whether he had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After Slobodan Dubocanin had questioned you and then they started to punch you and kick you, did they do anything else to you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, Slobodan Dubocanin took his pistol out. He showed it to me. Then he rolled the Chamber and said: "Let's see how lucky you are." He then pointed a gun at my temple, and I expected him to pull the trigger at any time. I didn't know whether it was a game or whether it was part of the tactics they used in the course of the interrogation. I took it seriously, and at that time life came to a halt for me. Time simply stopped. All sorts of images from my earlier life passed through my mind, and everything was very confused, and I couldn't understand anything. I didn't understand what was happening to me. Then I heard the sound of a click, and it was as if I had come to my senses at that time. But it didn't end with that. Slobodan Dubocanin took out a knife and put it to my right eye. He then pulled my head back and I felt such pain that I fainted. I felt my eye had left my body and that it was no longer part of me. The pain was difficult to endure, and I fainted. I was completely unaware of what was happening at that time. I still feel the consequences of this act. I still have problems with seeing with my right eye, because ... I have double image as a result of all the blows that I had been dealt, I almost went blind in my right eye. It was almost impossible for me to see anything with my right eye. I could only see a little. And if I wanted to see something, I had to cover that eye with my hand in order to be able to discern anything. I felt pain all over my body. I wasn't able to move my hands or legs freely. I Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17821 to 17828. felt almost paralysed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we continue or would you like a break?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to go back to the incident with the gun for one moment. Did Slobodan Dubocanin also place the barrel of the pistol in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I really didn't know whether it was a game or whether it was the way they were trying to get me to tell them something that I didn't know. I don't know whether someone was just amusing himself or whether this represented a real threat to my life. But for me, it was serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, unless I'm wrong, I don't think the witness has told us whether the pistol that Dubocanin was using was loaded or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he has said that. But in his statement, details which perhaps you can go straight to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, when Dubocanin pulled out the pistol, did he show you an empty chamber?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He first showed me that the chamber was full, and then he emptied the chamber, and then he put a bullet back in the chamber. I couldn't see where he put the bullet in the chamber. At the time it wasn't possible for me to see that. I wasn't in a position to see all those details. But I'm persuaded that the bullet was in the chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see him roll the chamber around at all?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that, and I heard him doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This pistol, I take it, was a revolver, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you --

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a magnum. I don't know what the calibre was. I think it had a large calibre, perhaps a 9-millimetre-calibre pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you said that when you were -- when Dubocanin cut you with the knife above your right eye, you said you fainted. When you regained consciousness, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They took me down the stairs. I think it was a room, an isolation cell of some sort. I don't know where it was, but first they took me to a corridor. I was left standing in the corridor, facing the wall, with my legs spread out. I had to lean against the wall with three fingers. All the people who passed by would beat me in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were these people that beat you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They always came in groups of three or four men, never alone. I wasn't able to turn around to see their faces, so I can't describe them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to see how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, he mentions three fingers on each hand. Did that have any significance to him? Did that mean anything, using three fingers only and not four or five or two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, because it's a well-known fact that Serbs greet each other with three fingers, so I had to lean against the wall with three fingers and remain in that position. So I was being humiliated as a Muslim, as a Bosniak, because I had to use or accept this Serbian form of greeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before these people came past in groups of three or four, did you hear anything over the loudspeaker?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Since from the place where I stood less five metres away from that place there was the policeman on duty, and he used the radio to say that he had a Mujahedin with him and if they wanted to see him, that they should come. After -- a few minutes later, a group, a small group came and so it went on and on and on, so that I lost count. I really didn't know how many people were meeting me and where. And they were hitting me. I thought that those were the orders, but my body was doubling under the blows, and I was falling down on the floor, and I would be straightened up, how many times, Your Honours, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you were then taken to an isolation cell of some sort in the basement.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That room that they took me to, I went down some stairs and I assume that it was a solitary confinement cell, because it was in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you stay in that room overnight?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you interrogated the following day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who by?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The same inspector, Zdravko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did the interrogation last that day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
