utterances.text: Throughout the working hours, and I was taken to the corridor and brought back a number of times, so I cannot give you a precise answer. I don't know. But I was brought into that room several times that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When the interrogation finished, where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: And then they transferred me to the elementary school, which was near the police station, and we were put -- I was put in a gym.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any other detainees there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. On the other side, there were some 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these men?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know who was in charge of the people being detained at the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: As a rule, there was a man whom I used to know as a waiter at Plasa. That's a pub which is called Plasa. And we used to call him Pop. So Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many guards were at the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: There would always be one at the entrance to the school; others I could not see. I mean, at the entrance to the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They wore police clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see that. But on one occasion, I saw one holding a weapon. But when they were coming into the gymnasium, I couldn't see if they had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these guards?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the already mentioned waiter, I didn't know anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Later that evening, were your names read out?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened during that first night that you were in the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You mean the roll-call?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened after the roll-call? Were you then taken again -- were you taken from the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: After the roll-call, I was taken to a part of the building which was used as lockers, as dressing rooms for the children, for the pupils, before and after going to the gym, where showers were and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point that night, were you taken from the school, and the following morning you woke up in the police station?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I woke up in a room, and I thought it was in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is it right that you had fainted before you knew that you were in the police station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't really stated or confirmed that it was the police station that he found himself in in the morning. He says that he thought it was. So I will ask him the same question without making it or putting words in his mouth which he hasn't stated as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, that night, did something happen to you and you fainted?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to the bathroom, and there they started striking me, and I passed out. And I really don't know where my body was taken from there, because during this torture, I passed out frequently. And whenever I woke up, it was a new day to me; that is, I lost all idea of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you woke up in the morning, where were you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I was in a room which was very small. I think it was in the cellar, somewhere below the ground level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you at some point -- and was that in the police station?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I'd say yes, because there was nowhere else they could take me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Mileka Dotic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many other men were there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: There was a group of about 15 to 20 individuals. There was some noise, but I didn't know what it was about. And Mileka Dotic was one of those in the group whom I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were the other members -- how was he and the other members dressed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They were all in camouflage police clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you at some point taken inside the police station building?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment, I didn't realise what was going on, but at that moment, a somewhat younger policeman came and took me back to the room from which they had taken me out. I did not know at that time why I had been taken back, but whatever, I was taken back to that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before you were -- you go on to discuss that, were you beaten in this room with these 15 to 20 individuals?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Those 15 to 20 men were in front of the police station, not in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go back. I think you need to go a little bit direct here. Go back to Mr. Mileka Dotic, the Mileka Dotic who you said you recognised amongst this group, do anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That gentleman, Mileka Dotic, tried to walk through this group and reach me, and I realised that he wanted something. But at that moment, I heard some words, kill, slaughter, or something, but I didn't really know what it was all about. And in that situation, I just stood. I didn't know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were you beaten by anyone on that occasion when Mileka Dotic said something that you're not quite sure about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it all happened so quickly, so that I don't know whether anyone struck me at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from there you said you were then taken to an office inside the police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you introduced to anybody?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I was taken to a man who said he was Nenad Balaban. I had never seen that man before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you questioned by Nenad Balaban?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of questions did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I went through the same procedure, who I am, what I am, same kind of questions which I already mentioned, except that I had to sign the official record of what I -- and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, if I'm reading the statement, the witness statement well, the Balaban incident, when Balaban, in other words, comes into the picture, happened quite a few days after.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So I suggest you bring back the witness to where you want him, and that was immediately after he had seen Mileka Dotic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, after you had seen Mileka Dotic and you were taken to an office inside the building, were you introduced to someone called Zaric, nicknamed Djiba?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The man who took me away from that group where Mileka Dotic was took me away from -- that is, somebody must have pushed them away, somebody, because I couldn't really move. And he just pushed those people away from me and took me back into the building. I didn't know Goran Zaric at the time. It was only later that I came across him again and learned that he was Goran Zaric. At that time, all that I heard was his nickname, Djiba.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So at that time, you were taken inside the police station?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, back into the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did Slobodan Dubocanin and others enter the office that day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The first instant, I didn't see Slobodan Dubocanin, but later on I did, and Slobodan Dubocanin started asking me about things which I had no idea about. And finally, he ordered me to lie down, and after that he tried to dance a folk reel on my body. And but it hurt so much that I passed out. And how long it lasted, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was Dubocanin, was he the only one that mistreated you on that occasion, or the other men as well?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: There were others, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many others?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Well, not -- at least two or three men, because Slobodan Dubocanin never came alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go directly -- you can mention the name to him and ask him whether this person beat him up as well. I'm referring to a certain Bojic, whose first name is not known.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, when you regained consciousness, were you introduced to a man called Bojic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Bojic wore the camouflage police uniform, athletic build, medium height. He was rather dark-skinned. His complexion was dark and his hair was black. Something that I didn't notice before that: He tried to beat me alone, and I tried to protect myself, and then he called to some people to come and help him, so that they just held me tight and he beat me, and I then passed out again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you're referring to medium height, approximately how tall is that? Because I know that you are very tall. So what do you call "medium height"?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Well, to me, it is between 175 and 180 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By standard in that area in the world, I would be a midget Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, were you again interrogated by Inspector Zdravko?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time, because I don't know when I was let go, those before him [as interpreted]. So that when I came to, I was brought to this room once again for further interrogation, but I cannot give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again, were the questions the same or different?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The questions were the same, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you given anything in newspaper?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: At some point while Zdravko was interrogating me, two men came in. Whether he invited them to come or not, I don't know. But two men in camouflage uniforms came, and one of the two was saying how they had killed my brother. And I knew that he had been captured, but I didn't know where he was. And I thought that perhaps he was in a different prison, because I couldn't really know how many facilities there were where people were detained. And he showed me some fingers which had been cut off recently. You could see blood on them. And he said: These are your brother's fingers. We killed him just a few moments ago. And I looked at those fingers. I just cast a look at them. But at that moment, of course, I couldn't know whether they were Ahmet's fingers. I thought they were not, and I was hoping that they were not his fingers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After this incident, did Slobodan Dubocanin and Vujicic enter the room?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What occurred after they entered the room?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Whenever Slobodan Dubocanin entered, a new round of torture for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What occurred on this occasion? What did he do to you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember. It escapes me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. We move to the next incident, Ms. Sutherland. You don't have to worry if, Mr. Cirkic, if you don't remember anything in particular. You're not standing trial here; you're just giving evidence. So you don't have to worry. No one will blame you if you have forgotten some of these facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, at some point I think you fainted again. And when you woke up, what wounds did you notice?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I noticed that my lip was cut, and it was bleeding profusely. And I tried to somehow put this piece back, but that cut piece just hung there. It was a long cut, a cut long, two or three centimetres, and you can still see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After this, were you returned to the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we talked earlier this morning about the 17 to 20 men getting killed in Dabovci. Is that where you were told about that, in this school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in that very school. I do not know the exact date, but I think it was sometime between the 17th or maybe 18th of August, and I received this information from a man whom I knew before, that is, his name is Alija Cejvan. At some point, Alija came to me and tried to talk with me, and I told him: Don't talk with me, because you could get beaten and it won't be good for you. But he didn't obey me, and went on talking. And so he gave me several names of persons who had been killed, but I do not remember those names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you mistreated while you were detained at the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly for the Court what happened?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have the impression that I was being beaten all the time. I don't know how long were the breaks between the beatings. My body hurt all over. I felt as somebody who was completely paralysed. I couldn't move. I could barely move my arms. And I've already told you as regards my sight. My body was on the brink at that time. I could not stand the pain any longer. At those moments I thought that death was the only way out for me. I simply couldn't see any other way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident which occurred in the locker room?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once I was taken to the locker room for interrogation, they left me there unconscious. After a period of time, I could hear screams. I could hear voices. And I tried to focus, to find out where I was and what was going on. And at that moment, I noticed several policemen. I don't know the exact number - and two Croats who were being interrogated about something. I recognised one of those Croats, (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: was being accused of having built an electric chair to torture and kill the Serbs. And he kept denying it and saying that he knew nothing about such things. The other one, they were trying to extort some money or some gold from the other one, saying that he had buried it somewhere. And he was saying that he didn't have any, that he was of medium standard. But those who interrogated them were not very satisfied with the answers, and after a period of beating they forced them to engage in anal sex. I tried to see what was happening. When I saw what was going on, I tried somehow to pull back and pretend that I was still unconscious, to avoid being beaten again. And I saw them pulling down their trousers. But as I said, I tried to pull back a little. And throughout the time, I pretended I was unconscious, in order to avoid any risk to myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point, were you taken again back to the police station to Inspector Zdravko's office?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I was taken back to Inspector Zdravko's office, but I think that Inspector Zdravko was not there on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you hear people being interrogated and beaten at the police station?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard once people who were to testify that they knew me. Those people were beaten and asked if they knew me, and people said they didn't. But after a while, they were forced to say that they did know me. Whether and how much those people really knew me, that is something I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Going back to the school, how often, if at all, did special unit members come to the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they came. And as far as I can remember, I'd say they came every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what made them different from the regular policemen?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They wore some hats, like camouflage hats, and had uniforms which were green. They didn't look like those blue uniforms that regular policemen wore.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of these special units?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Dubocanin introduced himself as the special troops captain. I don't know whether he was really the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you were interrogated by Nenad Balaban and that he gave you a document. What was that document about?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Balaban appeared with some documents that were supposed to be my statement that I was supposed to sign and to admit that what was contained in the statement was true and that I stood by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you read the document and sign the document?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't in a position to read it, nor was I in a position to sign it. I really tried to sign it, to put an end to everything. I was no longer able to endure this. But I was prepared to sign the statement, regardless of its contents. I took the pen that I was provided with in order to sign the statement, but I dropped the pen. At that point, another man sitting on the side, sitting by Balaban, he stood up. He was a little older and was greying. But he was also wearing a police camouflage uniform. Balaban had a look at me and then asked me what was that on your lips? I said I fell down the stairs and cut myself. And then Balaban said that I was lying. I said that that was the truth. And then Balaban ordered me to take my shirt off. That was the first time that I had a look at my body without my shirt on. I couldn't even see white skin anywhere. Everything was dark blue and yellow. Balaban ordered me to turn around, to turn my back to him, which is what I did. Then the two of them had a look, and he said: Very well. Get dressed. And he stopped at that point. He didn't insist on me talking about my cut lips.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make an application to have the names of the persons involved in the incident back at the school redacted for reasons of privacy, their privacy? So the incident still stays in the transcript, but the names of the individuals is redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution's request is being granted, registrar, and you will liaise with Ms. Sutherland to make sure that we redact the right names and not others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It's on page 54, lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could redact this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- Lines 3 to 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That should help you enough, Madam Registrar. Have you located them? Sorry. Yes, you can proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what happened after you got dressed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: After I got dressed, I don't know whether I tried to sign the record again, but Balaban ordered the other person to take me back to the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've mentioned one incident where detainees were mistreated. Were there any other incidents that you saw where detainees were mistreated back at the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: As there was a sports hall there, special troops came on several occasions. They wanted to play football with our people. Each time there were incidents, but I really can't remember certain things now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the conditions in the school? What were your sleeping arrangements? What was the food like? Were you able to wash daily?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I personally slept on the parquet. I was provided with a rubber ball as a pillow, which I wasn't able to use. I didn't have anything to lie on. I was right by the entrance to the hall. Others were at the opposite end, by the wall. I didn't notice -- I noticed that they had something that they could lie on, blankets or something like that. As far as food is concerned, we weren't provided with food regularly, and we weren't provided with a sufficient amount of food. I noticed that on several occasions, found that already had gone bad, was provided [as interpreted]. If you ate such food, you would have to suddenly rush to the toilet, because you could quite simply not keep this food down. As far as bathing is concerned, I never had a bath in the school, so I felt my own body odour. I could smell my own body odour. I really do not know whether other people had the opportunity to have a bath or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long were you detained in the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: About a month, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I meant to ask you this question earlier: What was the ethnicity of the man that you said was in charge of the school, Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that you weren't able to recognise any of the guards. But do you know their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't recognise that, but they were Serbs. There were only Serbs in the Serbian police force, because the Croats and the Muslims had been dismissed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Dule Vujicic, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of Inspector Zdravko?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know his ethnicity, but I assume that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Slobodan Dubocanin, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Dubocanin boasted that he was a Serb, a real Serb, so I'm sure that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After your detention in the school for a month, where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We were then taken to the old prison. It's a building behind the court building, in the municipality building. The local population called it the old prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was in the town of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2320.19, ERN number 0203-3442.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You can see the building of the municipality, the municipal building here, and the prison building is on the other side. It's behind this part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were just pointing then with the pointer to the right-hand corner of the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that street there led up to the building where the old prison was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened when you entered the prison?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Our names were entered in a register. Our names were recorded. I don't know whether the date was recorded. And we were placed in two rooms. Some of us went to a room called number 3, whereas others were taken to a room marked as room number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many other detainees were at the old prison?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: You mean in both rooms?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: At the time there were between 70 and 75 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one question going back to the school. Were you ever provided any medical attention, you or any of the other detainees, for the injuries which you suffered, you sustained?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I personally wasn't provided with any medical assistance. I don't know about others. The only medical assistance I was provided with in the school was assistance provided by a detainee. He had graduated from medical faculty, or was supposed to graduate. He offered to sew up my cut, but the guards refused to allow him to do so. And then I was given some tablets, some pills, some painkillers. And then there was someone called Ahmet Zulic, who provided with me with a handkerchief of some kind with which to cover my cut. But at that time, no, I wasn't provided with any medical treatment in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And were you allowed visits from outside?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I personally did not receive any visits, but some people did, some local inhabitants from Kotor Varos. Once a week they would receive a little food and some clothes. These visits were allowed when Goran Zaric was the warden of the prison. When he left, these visits came to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's my fault for confusing you. Were you allowed visits when you were at the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't, but as far as I can remember, some people went out with the guards for some parcels, but I didn't see the people who came to visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, going back to the old prison building behind the Municipal Assembly building, do you know who was in charge there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Goran Zaric, Djiba, was in charge of that prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I remember one of them who was well-known in Kotor Varos as Ljubo "Zilo". I don't know his surname. Tesic "Bedi" was the third person. I don't know whether that was his real name. The name of a fourth person was Aleksandar. They called him Aco. But I can't remember his surname right now. But I do know that they called him Aco.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Vucanovic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think his name was Aco Vucanovic. I think Vucanovic was his surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did these people do before the war? What was their occupation?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I can remember, only Goran Zaric, Djiba, was a policeman, whereas the others, I don't think that they were policemen. I think they were citizens employed in some companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Goran Zaric and the guards that you were able to recognise?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs. They were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the detainees ever taken out for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, except on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did anyone escape during this forced labour?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, people were taken away in the morning and they were returned about 12.00, as far as I can remember. Then there was some sort of confusion, and I -- some sort of alert, and I found out that from the neighbouring rooms, not from room number 2 -- I apologise. Not from room number 3 -- or room number 3 some people ran away. They all had the same surname, Sipura, Zoran, Jakica, and Svetko. So for a certain period of time there was no more labour. The guards were replaced immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were they replaced by? What were their names and their ethnicities, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Radenko Krejic. No. Radenko Keverovic, someone who introduced himself as Krejic. I don't remember his first name. Nedjo Djukic. And someone whose surname was Zutic. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what any of these men did before the war?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you at any time do forced labour?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: On one occasion I was taken to clean an area in front of the fire brigade centre, which at that time had been transformed into a barracks. When I was taken out with a group of people to do this work, the weather was bad. It was just before a storm. My first task was to gather the leaves. I took a broom. I tried to sweep the leaves up. But whenever I gathered some of these leaves, the wind would start blowing and scatter them. The person in charge of me started laughing, approached the vehicle, put some music on, and asked me whether I knew how to sing Serbian songs, and then started playing Serbian songs for me. I don't know how I managed to complete that task. The second task I had was to clean a mirror that had been stained. It was quite a big mirror. It was on the wall. I had been ordered to clean it so that it was shiny. Your Honours, I couldn't see my own image, my own reflection in that mirror, I was in such a bad state. But I took some sort of solutions. I tried to clean it. The person in charge of me moved a bit. A young man came to help me. He was a distant relative of me, Turan Dzevad. He quickly cleaned that part. Within -- taken behind that building to a sort of shack. There was some materials there. We were supposed to build some sort of area where we could roast pigs. My task was to take an axe and chop wood. I tried to chop the wood, but I couldn't hit the wood. I would raise the axe, but I kept missing, and this made the others laugh. I don't know what would have happened if Goran Zaric, Djiba, hadn't appeared at one moment, and he took me and one of the other men and returned me to the old prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While you were on this forced labour, did you overhear any soldiers talking about their pay or lack thereof?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: In front of the fire brigade, they centred -- two men in uniforms of the special police appeared. They started speaking to my guard and he then started swearing. They mentioned the name of Djeka, who had promised some sort of pay. Apparently their pays were late and they were saying: "We're good enough for them when it's necessary to fight, but when they have to pay us, there's no money." I heard this conversation by chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say they mentioned the name of Djeka. Did you know who they were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. Djekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know anyone by the surname Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't know the person by that name, but I know that Djekanovic had an important position in the police, in the municipality of Kotor Varos, and he was also a member of the parliament in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point were you registered by the ICRC while you were at the prison?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of us were registered, I think about 12 of us, whereas the others who were doing forced labour weren't registered, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did any new prisoners, detainees, arrive?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but in the afternoon, preparations were made in the prison. The rooms opposite my room were emptied. And at some point, we heard new people being brought in. I recognised who was in question, because it was possible to hear their voices. While they were being interrogated, we were forced to sing Serbian songs, which we had to practice regularly, because there was someone who was charged with training us. So when we finished singing one song, we would sing another one. And then someone would knock on the door and say: Sing it again. And we would start singing again. So we had to sing incessantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For approximately how long did this singing last for?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Well, until about midnight. I can't tell you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened the following morning, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: In the evening we had been forbidden to leave the room. In the morning, until we received the order. So spent a little more time in the cells, in the rooms. In the meantime, we heard some sort of noise. First you could hear a tractor arriving in front of the prison building, and then you could hear some people and the sound of some plastic bags. We then heard something happening in the corridor, or in one of the rooms opposite our room. And then something was taken out after that. I didn't know what was happening or what had happened at that point in time. In my opinion, someone had been killed in the prison and taken outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened later that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Maybe about 1500 hours - perhaps I'm wrong, but I think that was the time - three policemen entered, one of whom returned. One of them was Radenko. They approached Turan Dzevad and Amir Zec and told them that they had 15 minutes to get ready and that they were going to be involved in an exchange. After that, two policemen returned and approached someone whose name was Muharem Pasic. They asked him how old he was. He answered. They then said: That is convenient. That suits us. And they took him away too. I think that half an hour or an hour passed, and then Radenko returned. He approached me. He said: "Come on, now. You're leaving." I said: "Should I get ready?" He said: "No. You're ready." He took me outside. In front of the prison, there was a Golf, a vehicle. The driver was at the wheel, and the engine was running. They put me in the back. The car left in the direction of Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he tell you what was going to happen to you when he first walked into the room?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know I would be exchanged. He said they were going to kill me. I didn't know whether they were really taking me away to be killed or whether I was going to be exchanged. When the car headed in the direction of Vrbanjci, I then thought that there really might be an exchange, but since people had been killed before me, I thought that I wouldn't be exchanged. I wasn't sure what would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We need to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have approximately another five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think it's important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That should be enough for you, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's perfect. We will reconvene, hopefully, in 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we are going to be busy. It may well be possible that we might reconvene a little bit later. But let's hope we can reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cirkic, I apologise for having kept you waiting beyond what I told you before. The same applies to you, Ms. Sutherland, and to you, Mr. Cunningham, and all the others, but we were busy and we couldn't return earlier than that, although we did our best. So let's proceed. Please try to conclude, leaving Mr. Cunningham a good 30 minutes for his cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before we broke a moment ago, Mr. Cirkic, we were -- you were discussing how you were called out, and that you were put into a Golf motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We reached the main -- or rather, the high street in Kotor Varos, and then the Golf turned in the direction of Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you stop -- were you ordered to sing while you were in this car?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of those present ordered me to sing, and the other one said: Oh, let him be. He's sung enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think then you reached Vrbanjci, and you stopped at the cafe bar owned by Dzevad Alagic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the condition of the bar?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The cafe was in ruins. At the bar, one could see lots of broken bottles. There were broken chairs. And in front of the cafe too. I mean, it was in terrible shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Dzevad Alagic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: A Bosniak, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Inside the bar, did you see Dzevad Turan and Amir Zec?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And these people had been detained with you in the prison?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you didn't see Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After a short while, did someone called Fra Adolf show up, holding a white flag?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he ask Keverovic if he had brought you, which he then confirmed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you asked by this Fra Adolf your name, and you confirmed -- you told him your name?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he told you that you would be exchanged for Nedjeljko Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is it correct that his son Nevenkao Djukic had arranged for the exchange to occur?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: From what I gathered, it was his son who had organised the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you had to meet each other halfway between the coffee bar and Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, Judge. Can I change headphones? Mine's going in and out with the translation. Can I have just a minute to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You had to meet each other halfway between the coffee bar and Vrbanjci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Between the coffee bar and the bridge over the River Mlava. I mean, when you say Vrbanjci, it could be anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And there was a group of between 40 and 50 Serb soldiers near you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were in the coffee bar and others were around the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before you started to walk, were you introduced to two people, one Zdravko Pejic, who introduced himself as the chief of police in Kotor Varos, and the other Sasa Petrovic, who introduced himself as the commander of a military unit located in Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Before we set off towards the line where we were to be exchanged, I was approached by two uniformed men. And this is Sasa Petrovic, sorry. What I see here, it says here something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript has another first name, has another name. And you were told not to say anything about your treatment that you had received during your detention?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: We were given those instructions earlier, that we were to say that we had been treated normally, that nothing untoward had happened, that there was an exchange, which meant a positive step forward, and that we should not talk about what we had been through or seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the date that you were exchanged was on or about the 30th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From there --

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I believe it would be the date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From there, is it correct that you arranged to travel to Travnik in a convoy?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you very briefly tell the Judges what happened on the day that you had to board the bus.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Before we were to board the bus, lists of people to be transferred from the -- from Vrbanjci to Travnik were to be compiled, had to be compiled, and these lists were to be handed over next to the Catholic church in Vrbanjci, and from there, they went to Kotor Varos, and then the next day the buses came and the transport was organised then. I don't know who put me on their list, but I heard that that day I should -- I would be leaving the neighbourhood community of Vrbanjci with a group. I can't give you the exact number. But that there were between six or eight buses full of people leaving Donji Vrbanjci. One group returned because there was no room for them. All the others were searched in a building, in one house men were frisked; and in another, women; and then they were being directed towards buses which had numbers 1 to 3. So I was put on a bus, but before boarding the bus itself, I once again came across Sasa Petrovic and Balaban, and I think that Balaban was accompanied by a man from Vecici called Raif Alagic. And I think they were conducting negotiations at the moment that Vecici should be -- that the population in Vecici should be moved out in some way. But I didn't know more about that at the time. And as we were entering the buses, in front of the bus that I was to board, there was a bench, and on that bench, there were three persons sitting. I think it was a woman in the middle and two men, and one of those individuals, I think I had met him before, and his name was Sinisa, and he used to work at the Cadastre, at the land registry office. I don't know what he did there. And we were supposed to pay the fare there and sign that -- sign over the property that we had. What that receipt said, I couldn't really read it, so I merely signed it, paid the fare, and headed for the bus. And at that moment, Balaban came to me once again and said: It would be good if the two of us could meet at some other time and talk with persons who were in charge of the escort of the bus. So I boarded the bus, but the bus was full. I went to the other bus which was not filled. But those people who couldn't find room on any bus, they were taken back to Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this form that you had to fill out, was it in Cyrillic or Latin script?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The form was in Cyrillic, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as far as you know, did it say that the form that you signed, was it signing over your property voluntarily to the Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not read that statement, but from what I know, everybody who was leaving had to sign such a statement. But I had neither time nor opportunity nor strength enough to read it. I simply signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the people that were there, the man from the land office, did they fill out the details on the form, your details?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The form that I see had already been filled. All I had to do was put my signature there. All rest was already printed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how much did you have to pay to go on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: At some point, I was told it would be 100 marks, but the prices were from 100 marks for adults, 50 marks for children. I gave them a hundred-mark note, and I didn't get any change back, and that is why I think that the price was 100 marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It was in Vecici that I learnt, that day when I came out of the camp, that my children were in Bilice and that they had taken the convoy towards Travnik. That wasn't a reliable information, but that was what people told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did you -- when did this convoy of buses that you were on leave Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Month?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I think, however, that it was around 3.00, perhaps a little later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What month did you travel?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I think that the exact date was the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These buses then left Kotor Varos --

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: But I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the buses then left Kotor Varos and drove to a place called Smetovi, and you were told that you had to walk from there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's approximately 20 kilometres to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how many kilometres, but I know I had to walk quite a long time, because everybody else who had got off their bus overtook me, and I was in a pretty bad shape, so that I was one of the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you arrived in Travnik, did you stay in a medical centre for approximately one month?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did people come to visit you and tell you things that had happened in the Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, although I was in a very bad shape, I tried to move around, so that I communicated with quite a number of people while I was in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Akif Pasic, did he visit you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Akif Pasic was brought a few days later. He was brought by two men. He was practically -- he collapsed. I mean, he couldn't walk on his own. And he was in this very bad state, very bad condition, for a few days. And after that, he told me about his journey from Vecici to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he tell you about an incident that occurred in Grabovica on the 3rd of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Akif Pasic told me, not in so many words, that they left in late afternoon, that they came across an ambush, that they split into small groups, and that with his group, he separated from others, and that they heard gunfire and that one group had been taken in the direction of Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that other group?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: They were never seen again. Your Honours, a group of women were also taken with that group of men. The next day, those women were brought to Travnik, and those women told me and Akif, because Akif went to ask them, because his two brothers had gone missing, and so he went to ask what had happened to those people, and they were told that they had stayed behind in the school in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were in this group?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: The first figure was -- the initial figure was 180 men, and then we heard that in the Skender Vakuf municipality, some were captured, others were captured in the territory of Donji Vakuf municipality, so that the number of persons who went missing in the area of Grabovica was somewhere between 162, 163 persons. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did a person called Drago Bandala from Bilice tell you about a massacre that occurred in the mosque in Hanifici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I was lying in the hospital in Travnik, Drago Bandala, who had found temporary accommodation in the neighbouring municipality of Vitez and come to see me, told me about what had happened in the mosque in Hanifici and Cirkici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did a person called Hasan Vilic tell you that he buried the bodies of six women and one man from a massacre that occurred in Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes, Hasan Vilic is from my village. There were three -- two or three households where that last name Cirkic and the village was set on fire. He came in the late afternoon and he found cow sheds that were burnt down, the bodies of six women and one man, and he recognised his mother by a ring on the finger of one of those bodies. And he also recognised my wife's brother, Aziz. Aziz was a mentally disabled person. He was retarded. And he usually had some small souvenirs, lighters or something, with him, and that is how he recognised him, because he had rubber boots, so he thought it might have been his body. So he put them all in a sack or something and buried them behind the village, in a plot that he owned. That is what I heard from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Cirkic. I was trying to rush. What were you told from Drago Bandala about the massacre in the mosque in Hanifici?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Drago Bandala said that a few minutes after the Serb units had left that area, he came with a group of people and saw the mosque in -- burning. And he said sometime before that he heard some shots in that area. And when he entered the mosque, part of that mosque started burning, that is, the rugs in the mosque. Which -- so the mosque had been torched. And he saw bodies of several persons in one corner of the mosque and he got those bodies out and buried them. He tried to put the fire out, and he managed to do it with the help of some others, so that the mosque did not burn at the time. But he also found many bullet casings in the mosque, in the mosque where people go to pray.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stayed in Travnik for approximately one month; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from there you went to Karlovac, in Croatia, where you stayed for approximately eight months?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from there you went to a third country?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 or 1993 -- or beginning of 1993, did you compile a list of persons who were detained in Kotor Varos from the Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I tried to recall all the persons whom I saw in the prison, and I compiled a list of those names. Unfortunately, many of them I didn't know before, or rather, I knew only the nicknames or the last names of various people. After that, I established contact with Bakir Dizdar and I told him that it would be a good idea, and he undertook to do it. So he took those lists from me and also took two other people trying to add names to the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm doing my best, but Mr. Cunningham certainly is not going to have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This strengthens my conviction how necessary it is for me, as President of this Trial Chamber, to set out a time limit within which you have to finish. Because five to ten minutes became already 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This was a witness which you yourself, the Prosecution, anticipated would last one day, cross-examination included. And we aren't anywhere near that as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this witness's evidence has been very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not contesting the importance, and that's why I'm letting you continue. I haven't stopped you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown this document. It has an ERN number 0045-6995. And Your Honour, copies have already been -- copies are here for distribution. A copy has been provided to the Defence. It was disclosed some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please have a look at that document. Is this the list that you helped compile with Bakir Dizdar and another gentleman called Seval Alagic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many names contained on this list were you able to recall?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I think over 50 per cent of the names of the people I met. In some cases our lists overlapped. We compiled the same lists. We tried to correct this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And these people are listed under the village that they came from within the Kotor Varos municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If this document -- originally marked P2121, Your Honour. Sir, I've finished with that document. I just have three or four more questions for you. You have mentioned the problems with your eyesight. What -- do you suffer from any other long-term health problems as a result of what happened to you during your detention at the police station, the school, and the old prison in Kotor Varos in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I feel any changes in the weather, in my back, in the area of my back. Then there are the consequences I have already mentioned. In addition, I have three broken ribs which have healed as they were left fractured. But when I do difficult physical labour, this causes me pain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think you also said that you have a number of broken teeth.

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot about my teeth. When I arrived in the third country, the authorities offered to repair my damaged teeth. Some of them were treated. So I now no longer have problems with my teeth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many relatives did you lose in 1992 because of what happened in Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: From the core family members, I lost two family members. And two or three people from my extended family. About five family members in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were they killed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I know that one of them was hit by a shell in Vecici. The others are listed as missing, in Grabovica. So I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many relatives did your wife lose?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: My wife lost two brothers, an aunt, an uncle, two of their sons. Then the children from that family, nephews; and then the family that lost some people in Vecici, I think that a total of 15 members of her family died in the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you write your memoirs about what happened to you and about what happened in the Kotor Varos municipality in 1994?

utterances.speaker: RASIM CIRKIC
utterances.text: I tried to put a few things down on paper. Your Honours, I was never able to correct the grammatical mistakes or certain other things. This material is in a very raw state. I was never able to make corrections to it. That would remind me of everything, and that's something that I don't want to do. What I wrote down, a lot of it is information that I heard. I gathered information, where I was in Croatia, and I tried to conjure up some sort of a picture of the events in the municipality of Kotor Varos. That would be a work of a more literary nature. I'd like to try to go through that, but unfortunately I didn't find the force to establish contact with some people who might have other information or who might be able to correct me. But if such a person could be found, I would be very grateful to that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, do you prefer to start now? We have six, seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't been able to find a witness for Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what worries me, Ms. Sutherland, and please do understand, this is what worries me. You can't find Mr. Treanor, who works with the OTP, Mr. Brown, who works with the OTP? They can't be brought, either of them, on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the two people that are leading those two witnesses have been out of the office for the past week and a half. They would need to prepare for both of those testimonies and I don't think they're going to be able to do it in 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very difficult for me to understand. I have spent the last over 30 years as a lawyer and a judge, and this is the first time that I hear that something like that cannot be prepared in 48 hours, especially with two experts, expert witnesses, having a report, an expert report which goes into hundreds and hundreds of papers which supposedly whoever is going to lead those witnesses knows precisely the contents of, better than we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's also a matter of determining which out of the hundreds of documents that are footnoted in the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just present the report. Otherwise I will deal with you the way you were dealt with in other cases, telling you we don't need expert reports. I come from a jurisdiction, Ms. Sutherland, where we don't even allow expert witnesses, ex parte expert witnesses, in criminal cases. And I can tell you here and now that irrespective of where they are going to come from, whether from your side or from the Defence, they are always going to be considered ex parte. So I suggest you don't waste much time. We do need them. I'm not saying that we don't need them. But they will be given the importance of ex parte.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was simply mentioning that we didn't have a witness for Friday before Mr. Cunningham makes his mind up whether he wanted to start examination this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose we can stop here. We take up the cross-examination tomorrow. And I will decide tomorrow whether the testimony of the next witness should end tomorrow or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's expected that he will finish within the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I hope so. Thank you, and we will reconvene tomorrow at 9.00. Yes. One moment. In the meantime, at some point in time between today and tomorrow, please try to go through the list of witnesses that you have given us for next week, for the coming week, so that we are assured that we don't have a repetition of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want Friday to be dedicated for reorganising the work for the week after, I'm pretty much prepared to grant you that. But otherwise, let's not waste a day like that. 9.00 tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
